lesson.grammar_point: describing trends: verbs and nouns of change with by, to, of and from

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to stop rising or falling and stay at about the same level
a sudden, short rise that quickly falls back
a list that shows how a total is divided into its parts
compared with the same period in the previous year
a value that is far away from all the others
to fall very fast and very far
to go up and down in an irregular way

paras: For the first time in a decade, the number of new cases filed with the center went down. Registrations fell by 12 percent year on year, from 243 in 2024 to 214 in 2025. Read on its own, that figure suggests a quieter year. It was not. The total amount in dispute rose to 9.6 billion reais, a threefold increase on the year before, and the average claim more than tripled. The center handled fewer cases, but the cases it handled were much larger.

The monthly figures tell the same story with more drama. New filings fluctuated between 14 and 21 a month for most of the year, peaked at 31 in March, when a wave of construction claims arrived together, and plummeted to six in July. The March spike is easy to explain: several contracts signed during the infrastructure program of 2021 reached their completion dates in the same quarter, and the disputes followed. The July figure is harder. Part of it is the winter recess; the rest, the report admits, is not yet understood.

The breakdown by sector shows where the growth came from. Construction disputes surged by 40 percent and now make up a third of the caseload. Technology disputes, which had grown steadily for five years, leveled off at around 30 cases. Corporate and M&A matters were stable. One case deserves its own sentence: a single energy claim of 2.3 billion reais accounts for almost a quarter of the total amount in dispute. Remove that outlier, and the increase is closer to twofold than threefold. The report's conclusion is cautious: the market is not shrinking, it is concentrating, and one year is not yet a trend.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson in the register of the annual report of an arbitration center

listenings.text: Every Monday I write about one number, and this week the number is the price of coffee. If you buy it in a supermarket in Europe, you have probably noticed. Over the last eighteen months, the wholesale price of arabica beans has more than doubled. It rose slowly through the spring, then surged in the summer, when a drought in Brazil cut the harvest. It peaked in February at its highest level in almost fifty years. Since then it has fallen by about a fifth, and many readers have written to me asking why the price on the shelf has not fallen with it. The answer is that supermarkets buy months in advance. The price you pay today reflects the beans that were bought at the peak. So my advice is simple. Do not look at one month. Look at the line, and remember that the shelf is always about six months behind the market.

I spend most of my working life making charts, and I want to tell you the three tricks I see every week. The first one is the axis that does not start at zero. A rise from ninety-eight to one hundred and two looks like a mountain if the axis starts at ninety-five. It is a change of four percent. The second trick is choosing the start date. If you want a line to look like it is going up, start it at the lowest point. Every price in the world surged after the bottom of a crisis. The third is the average that hides an outlier. One enormous number can turn a flat year into a record year. So before I believe any chart, I ask three questions. Where does the axis start? Why does the line start there? And what happens if you take the biggest number out? If nobody can answer, the chart is not information. It is an argument.
